title: Construction contracts by contractor: who needed a commission to raise the price
question: Among builders with several construction contracts in a department, does any need commission-approved increases more often than others on like work there, by more than chance would give?
finding: The commission items on disk cover 529 contracts; 248 are fixed-price construction contracts, 110 of those have a first and a latest figure, and their median rise is 19% (43 rose by a quarter or more). Job-order contracts are left out: 29 of the 65 on file were raised by exactly half, the one-time increase to $7.5 million that the Budget and Legislative Analyst describes as an option in the Administrative Code. Set against every fixed-price construction contract the same department held open in the same years, the share that needed a commission-approved increase is: Public Works 23 of 297 (8%); Public Utilities Commission 45 of 276 (16%); Airport 8 of 143 (6%); Port 8 of 59 (14%). Municipal Transportation Agency is left out of this test: the contract table keys too few of its contracts as construction to give a denominator. 43 contractor-and-department pairs hold five or more such contracts. 3 of them needed increases more often than their department's rate at the one-in-twenty level, where about 2.1 would by chance: Sierra Mountain Construction Inc at Public Utilities Commission (6 of 14, against 16%); Pilot Construction Management Inc at Airport (3 of 12, against 6%); Mitchell Engineering at Public Utilities Commission (4 of 8, against 16%). That is no more than chance. And among the 66 measured contracts whose builder has another measured one, the builder's other contracts predict a rise of a quarter or more worse than the department does (error 0.272 against 0.234; 0.229 knowing neither).
how: The commissions that oversee construction (Public Utilities, Airport, Port, Public Works since late 2022, and the transit Board) vote on contract changes above what staff may approve, and on close-outs; those items were read into one record per contract number and department. The first figure is the original amount where an item prints it (or, for the Public Utilities Commission, the award in its minutes); otherwise it is the amount that stood before the first change on file, which already includes earlier staff-approved changes and so understates growth. The latest figure is the final amount at close-out, or the total in the latest item. Where the Board of Supervisors approved the same change as a commission, the commission's row is kept and the Board's dropped; where a numbered modification appears twice, the later row is kept. Design-build and construction-manager contracts, which grow as phases and work packages are added, and professional-services contracts are kept apart from fixed-price construction. For each contractor and department: the construction contracts it held in the Supplier Contracts table that were open on or after the first date of that department's commission records on disk; how many of its contracts drew a commission-approved increase in price; the department's rate for all contractors; and the chance of that many or more at that rate. Contracts are listed where a contractor has three or more and at least one increase; the test counts those with five or more. The median rise and dollars added are over its contracts with a first and latest figure.
limits: Amounts and days are copied from agenda items and minutes and parsed from their wording; contractor names are phrases from the item text. A total in an item is an authorization, often including contingency, not money paid. Most Public Works rows are agenda items as proposed, because minutes before 2025 are not posted. A contract appears in these files only when a change needed a commission vote, so small changes approved by staff are invisible, and departments set that line differently: rates can be compared within a department, not across. Change orders for conditions found underground and for work the owner adds are an ordinary part of construction. The denominator comes from a different table than the numerator and the two are joined by contractor name, so a firm that appears under two spellings is undercounted on one side. A builder that takes the hardest jobs (deep sewers, old buildings, work beside live transit) will draw more changes for reasons that are not its doing. A commission-approved increase is not a finding against a contractor: several of the items say the City added the work.
